opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't put it exactly that way. It wasn't that Meta became a bad place. Meta has been extremely supportive of FAIR for more than a decade, and a lot of the work on self-supervised learning, on JEPA, on V-JEPA, came out of that environment. But there's a question of fit between the kind of research program you're pursuing and the priorities of the organization at a given time.

Over the last couple of years, the whole industry, Meta included, has been very focused on LLMs: scaling them up, shipping them in products, competing on chatbots. That's perfectly legitimate. LLMs are useful. But I've been saying for a long time that they are not the path to human-level intelligence. They don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan in the sense we need. To get there, you need systems that learn world models from sensory input like video, that can predict the consequences of their actions in an abstract representation space, and that can plan by optimizing objectives. That's what the JEPA architecture and objective-driven AI are about.

That program is a long-term one. It's going to take several years to mature, and it has applications far beyond what a social media and consumer company would naturally prioritize: robotics, industrial process control, healthcare, scientific modeling, things like that. So it made more sense to pursue it in a structure dedicated entirely to that mission, where the whole organization is aligned with this vision rather than being one research direction competing for attention and compute with a very large LLM effort.

Also, I think it's important that this work stays open. The kind of AI systems that will mediate all of our interactions with the digital world can't be controlled by a handful of companies. So the idea is to develop these world models, publish, open-source as much as possible, and work with partners, including Meta, to build them into actual products. It's not a divorce; it's more like the research had grown to a point where it needed its own home.

r001.rationale: The response says the industry, including Meta, focused on LLMs and that JEPA competed for attention and compute, but it does not identify a strategy of catching up with the industry as the cause.

r002.rationale: It says Meta’s focus on LLMs left the long-term JEPA and world-model program competing for attention and compute, and that the work needed an organization aligned with that mission.

r003.rationale: It says the program’s applications extend far beyond what a social media and consumer company would naturally prioritize, and gives robotics, industrial control, healthcare, and scientific modeling as examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first, let me be clear that I don't want this to sound like a complaint. I spent twelve years at Meta, I built FAIR from nothing, and it's one of the best industrial research labs in the world. I'm proud of that. But there's a difference between doing research and turning a research program into a product, and the second thing requires a kind of institutional focus that, frankly, had moved elsewhere.

The simple version is this: the entire industry, Meta included, went all in on large language models. Auto-regressive LLMs. And I've been saying for years, pretty loudly, that this is an off-ramp, not the highway. You cannot get to machines that understand the physical world, that have persistent memory, that can reason and plan, by predicting the next token. The LLM paradigm is extremely useful, I'm not dismissing it, but it is not a path to human-level intelligence. The research community mostly knows this. The money does not care.

So when the priorities shifted, when the company reorganized around superintelligence efforts built on top of that paradigm, with a very short time horizon and enormous pressure to ship, the JEPA work became something of an orphan. Not because people didn't believe in it. Many people inside did. But a world-model program is a five-to-ten-year bet. You need to train models that learn from video, that build abstract representations of the world, that plan in representation space rather than in text. That's not something you can staple onto next quarter's roadmap. And a large company, quite rationally from its point of view, allocates compute and people to what pays off soonest.

The other thing is structural. I was Chief AI Scientist, which is a wonderful title for doing research, but it's not a position from which you build a product line. In a big company, going from a paper to a product means passing through layers of product organizations with their own metrics, their own incentives, their own view of what a user wants this year. Each of those layers, reasonably, asks "why should we bet on this instead of the thing everyone else is doing?" And at some point you realize you're spending more energy on persuasion than on science.

So I concluded that the right structure for this was a focused organization, where the entire mission is world models. Where nobody has to be convinced that this is the goal, because it's the only goal. Where you can be patient, because patience is the whole plan. That's much easier to do as an independent entity than as a research group inside a company whose center of gravity is somewhere else.

And I'd add one more thing: I think it's healthy for the ecosystem. If everyone converges on the same architecture, with the same training recipe, we've essentially stopped exploring. Science needs people betting on different things. I've placed my bet. We'll find out if I'm right.

r001.rationale: The response says Meta joined the industry-wide shift to LLMs, but does not identify a strategy of catching up with the industry as the cause of reduced priority for exploratory research.

r002.rationale: It says Meta’s focus shifted to LLM-based superintelligence efforts and that the JEPA work became an orphan, making that organizational focus a barrier to advancing it.

r003.rationale: The response describes Meta’s short time horizon and different center of gravity, but does not state that most anticipated applications of the technology fell outside Meta’s interests.

astra-6.text: I’d question the premise a little. There’s a distinction between developing a research agenda and deciding how to turn it into products. JEPA and world models are a long-term research direction: learning representations that let a system predict what happens in the world and use those predictions to plan. That doesn’t, by itself, establish that Meta is the wrong place to pursue them. I wouldn’t attribute a departure or a particular business decision to that without first establishing what actually happened.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify Meta’s effort to catch up with the industry or say it reduced exploratory research priority.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Meta’s organizational focus on LLMs as a reason it was unsuitable for the work.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that most anticipated applications fell outside Meta’s interests.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate two questions: where to do the research, and where to turn it into products. Those aren’t necessarily the same organizational problem. But your question assumes that I concluded Meta was no longer the right place, and we haven’t established that premise. I wouldn’t want to invent a story about a departure or its reasons.

r001.rationale: The response gives no reason for reduced priority and does not mention Meta trying to catch up with the industry.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Meta’s focus on LLMs or connect it to the JEPA and world-model work.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether anticipated applications fell outside Meta’s interests.
